title: Bipolar Junction Transistors
description: npn and pnp transistors: current relations, operating regions, bias circuits and switching.

study.title: npn and pnp
study.body: A BJT has an **emitter**, **base** and **collector**. An npn has a thin p-type base between an n-type emitter and collector; a pnp is the reverse. The emitter arrow shows the direction of emitter current: out of the device for npn, into it for pnp. For npn, $i_B$ and $i_C$ are referenced into the device and $i_E$ out; for pnp all three directions are reversed, so the currents are positive in normal operation.

study.title: Current relations
study.body: KCL on the whole transistor: $i_E = i_B + i_C$. In the active region the collector current is $\beta$ times the base current ($\beta$ is typically 50–300, often about 100). The fraction of the emitter current that reaches the collector is $\alpha = \beta/(\beta + 1)$, slightly less than 1, so $i_C = \alpha i_E$.

study.title: Operating regions (npn)
study.body:
- **Cutoff:** both junctions reverse biased ($V_{BE} < 0.5$ V, $V_{BC} < 0.5$ V): $I_B = I_C = 0$.
- **Active:** base–emitter forward ($V_{BE} \approx 0.7$ V), base–collector reverse: $I_C = \beta I_B$. Valid if $I_B > 0$ and $V_{CE} > 0.2$ V.
- **Saturation:** both junctions forward: $V_{CE} \approx 0.2$ V. Valid if $I_B > 0$ and $\beta I_B > I_C > 0$.
For a pnp all voltage signs flip: $V_{BE} \approx -0.7$ V, active needs $V_{CE} < -0.2$ V, saturation $V_{CE} \approx -0.2$ V.

study.title: Fixed base bias
study.body: Assume active: $I_B = (V_{CC} - 0.7)/R_B$, $I_C = \beta I_B$, $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_C I_C$. Check $V_{CE} > 0.2$ V; if not, the BJT is saturated with $V_{CE} \approx 0.2$ V and $I_C = (V_{CC} - 0.2)/R_C$. Drawback: $I_C$ is proportional to $\beta$, so the Q point moves a lot between transistors.

study.title: Four-resistor bias
study.body: Replace the divider by its Thévenin equivalent: $V_B = V_{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, $R_B = R_1\|R_2$. The base loop $V_B = R_B I_B + 0.7 + R_E(\beta + 1)I_B$ gives $I_B$; then $I_C = \beta I_B$ and $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_C I_C - R_E I_E$. If $(\beta + 1)R_E \gg R_B$, then $I_C \approx (V_B - 0.7)/R_E$, almost independent of $\beta$.

study.title: The BJT as a switch
study.body: Input low: no base current, cutoff, $V_{CE} = V_{CC}$ (switch open). Input high: drive enough base current to **saturate** the transistor: $V_{CE} \approx 0.2$ V and $I_C = (V_{CC} - 0.2)/R_C$ (switch closed). Saturation requires $\beta I_B > I_C$, so $R_B < \beta(V_{in} - 0.7)/I_{C}$; designers usually overdrive the base by a factor 2 or more.

steps.title: Three terminals, two junctions
steps.body: A BJT has an emitter (E), base (B) and collector (C), forming two pn junctions: base–emitter and base–collector. In an **npn** the base is p-type, in a **pnp** it is n-type. A small base current controls a much larger collector current.

steps.prompt: In the circuit symbol of an **npn** transistor, the arrow on the emitter points…
options: out of the transistor, in the direction of the emitter current
from the collector to the base
the npn symbol has no arrow
steps.explanation: The arrow marks the emitter and shows the direction of emitter current, which is the forward direction of the base–emitter junction (p base to n emitter). For npn it points out; for pnp it points in.

steps.prompt: Tap the **emitter** of this pnp transistor.
steps.explanation: The emitter is the terminal with the **arrow**. In a pnp the arrow points **into** the transistor (from the p emitter into the n base), and the emitter is drawn at the top, because it connects to the more positive side. Node 3 is the base, node 2 the collector. (Memory aid: npn = "not pointing in".)

steps.title: Current relations
steps.body: In the active region the collector current is $\beta$ times the base current, and the emitter carries both (KCL):

steps.prompt: An npn transistor with $\beta$ = {{beta}} operates in the active region with $i_B$ = {{IB|A}}. Find $i_C$.
steps.explanation: $i_C = \beta i_B = {{beta}}\times{{IB|A}}$ = {{beta*IB|A}}.

steps.prompt: For the same kind of transistor ($\beta$ = {{beta}}, active, $i_B$ = {{IB|A}}), find the emitter current $i_E$.
steps.explanation: $i_C = \beta i_B$ = {{beta*IB|A}}, and KCL gives $i_E = i_B + i_C = (\beta + 1)i_B$ = {{(beta+1)*IB|A}}. The emitter current is only slightly larger than the collector current.

steps.title: Three regions
steps.body:
- **Cutoff:** both junctions reverse biased, no currents.
- **Active:** base–emitter forward ($V_{BE} \approx 0.7$ V), base–collector reverse; $I_C = \beta I_B$, needs $V_{CE} > 0.2$ V.
- **Saturation:** both junctions forward; $V_{CE} \approx 0.2$ V and $I_C < \beta I_B$.

steps.prompt: Match each npn operating region with its junction states
steps.explanation: The active region (BE forward, BC reverse) is the amplifier region where $I_C = \beta I_B$. Cutoff and saturation are the off and on states of a switch.

steps.prompt: An npn with $\beta$ = 100 has $I_B$ = {{IB|A}} and $I_C$ = {{IC|A}}, both positive. In which region does it operate?
steps.explanation: Both currents are positive, so it is not cut off. In the active region $I_C$ would equal $\beta I_B$ = {{100*IB|A}}. Here $I_C$ is smaller ($\beta I_B > I_C > 0$): the external circuit limits the collector current, so the transistor is **saturated**.

steps.prompt: For an npn transistor in the active region, $V_{CE}$ must be greater than about 0.2 V.
steps.explanation: Below about 0.2 V the base–collector junction becomes forward biased too and the transistor saturates. So the active-region model is valid only for $I_B > 0$ and $V_{CE} > 0.2$ V.

steps.prompt: The npn has $\beta$ = {{beta}}. Find the collector current $I_C$.
steps.explanation:
Assume active. Base loop: $I_B = \frac{V_{CC} - 0.7}{R_B} = \frac{ {{VCC}} - 0.7}{ {{RB}} }$ = {{IB|A}}.
$I_C = \beta I_B = {{beta}}\times{{IB|A}}$ = {{IC|A}}.
Check: $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_C I_C$ = {{VCE|V}} > 0.2 V ✓.

steps.prompt: Fixed base bias: $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}}, $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}}, $\beta$ = {{beta}}. Find $V_{CE}$ at the Q point.
steps.explanation:
$I_B = ({{VCC}} - 0.7)/{{RB}}$ = {{IB|A}}, $I_C = \beta I_B$ = {{IC|A}} (assuming active).
$V_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_C I_C = {{VCC}} - {{RC}}\times{{IC}}$ = {{VCE|V}}.
Since this is above 0.2 V, the active-region assumption holds.

steps.prompt: Measurements on an npn in the active region give $I_C$ = {{IC|A}} and $I_E$ = {{IE|A|4}}. Find $\beta$.
steps.explanation:
$I_B = I_E - I_C$ = {{IE|A|4}} − {{IC|A}} = {{IE-IC|A}}.
$\beta = I_C/I_B$ = {{IC}} / {{IE-IC}} = {{beta}}.
Small measurement errors in $I_E$ give big errors in $\beta$, because $I_B$ is a small difference.

steps.prompt: A transistor has $\beta$ = {{beta}}. Find $\alpha = I_C/I_E$ (give at least 3 significant figures).
steps.explanation: $I_E = (\beta + 1)I_B$ and $I_C = \beta I_B$, so $\alpha = \frac{\beta}{\beta + 1} = \frac{ {{beta}} }{ {{beta+1}} }$ = {{beta/(beta+1)||4}}.

steps.prompt: Fixed base bias with $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}}, $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}} and $\beta$ = 100. What is the operating point?
steps.explanation:
Assume active: $I_B = ({{VCC}} - 0.7)/{{RB}}$ = {{(VCC-0.7)/RB|A}}, $I_C$ = {{100*(VCC-0.7)/RB|A}}, so $V_{CE} = {{VCC}} - {{RC}}\times I_C$ = {{VCC-RC*100*(VCC-0.7)/RB|V}}: below 0.2 V, impossible.
Assume saturation: $V_{CE}$ = 0.2 V, $I_C = (V_{CC} - 0.2)/R_C$ = {{(VCC-0.2)/RC|A}}. Check $\beta I_B$ = {{100*(VCC-0.7)/RB|A}} > $I_C$ ✓.

steps.prompt: The pnp has $\beta$ = {{beta}} and operates in the active region ($V_{EB} \approx 0.7$ V). Find $V_{CE}$ (collector voltage minus emitter voltage).
steps.explanation:
The emitter is at {{VCC}} V and the base at $V_{CC} - 0.7$, so the base current flows **out** of the base through $R_B$: $I_B = ({{VCC}} - 0.7)/{{RB}}$ = {{IB|A}}.
$I_C = \beta I_B$ = {{IC|A}} flows out of the collector into $R_C$: $V_C = R_C I_C$ = {{VC|V}}.
$V_{CE} = V_C - V_E = {{VC}} - {{VCC}}$ = {{VC-VCC|V}}. Negative, and below −0.2 V, as required for an active pnp.

steps.prompt: With fixed base bias, replacing the transistor by one with twice the $\beta$ roughly doubles $I_C$ (as long as it stays active).
steps.explanation: $I_B = (V_{CC} - 0.7)/R_B$ does not depend on $\beta$, so $I_C = \beta I_B$ scales directly with $\beta$. That is why fixed base bias is a poor choice when $\beta$ varies; four-resistor bias fixes this.

steps.prompt: Four-resistor bias. To analyse it you replace the base circuit by its Thévenin equivalent ($V_B$, $R_B$). Tap the resistors that go into $V_B$ and $R_B$.
steps.explanation:
Cut the circuit at the base and look back towards the supply: you see the divider $R_1$–$R_2$. Its Thévenin equivalent is
$$V_B = V_{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad R_B = R_1 \parallel R_2$$
$R_C$ and $R_E$ are on the transistor side. $R_E$ appears in the base loop equation $V_B = I_B R_B + V_{BE} + I_E R_E$, but not in the Thévenin equivalent itself.

steps.prompt: Find $I_C$ for this four-resistor bias circuit ($\beta$ = {{beta}}, $V_{BE}$ = 0.7 V).
steps.explanation:
Thévenin of the divider: $V_B = {{VCC}}\frac{ {{R2}} }{ {{R1}} + {{R2}} }$ = {{VB|V}}, $R_B = R_1\|R_2$ = {{RB|Ω}}.
Base loop (active): $I_B = \frac{V_B - 0.7}{R_B + (\beta+1)R_E} = \frac{ {{VB-0.7}} }{ {{RB}} + {{beta+1}}\times{{RE}} }$ = {{IB|A}}.
$I_C = \beta I_B$ = {{IC|A}}. (Check: $V_{CE}$ = {{VCE|V}} > 0.2 V ✓.)

steps.prompt: Four-resistor bias: $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}}, $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}}, $\beta$ = {{beta}}. Find $V_{CE}$.
steps.explanation:
$V_B$ = {{VB|V}}, $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}}, $I_B = \frac{V_B - 0.7}{R_B + (\beta+1)R_E}$ = {{IB|A}}.
$I_C$ = {{IC|A}}, $I_E = (\beta+1)I_B$ = {{IE|A}}.
Collector–emitter loop: $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_C I_C - R_E I_E = {{VCC}} - {{RC*IC}} - {{RE*IE}}$ = {{VCE|V}}.

steps.prompt: What is the main purpose of the emitter resistor $R_E$ in four-resistor bias?
options: It makes $I_C$ nearly independent of $\beta$ when $(\beta+1)R_E \gg R_B$
It pushes the transistor into saturation
It removes the 0.7 V base–emitter drop
steps.explanation: With $(\beta + 1)R_E \gg R_B$, $I_E \approx (V_B - 0.7)/R_E$, which contains no $\beta$. The emitter resistor provides negative feedback: if $I_C$ tries to rise, $V_E$ rises, $V_{BE}$ margin shrinks and $I_B$ drops.

steps.prompt: In a four-resistor bias circuit ($V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}}), $\beta$ changes from 100 to 200. By what percentage does $I_C$ increase?
steps.explanation:
$V_B$ = {{VB|V}}, $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}}.
$\beta = 100$: $I_C = \frac{100({{VB-0.7}})}{ {{RB}} + 101\times{{RE}} }$ = {{I1|A|4}}.
$\beta = 200$: $I_C = \frac{200({{VB-0.7}})}{ {{RB}} + 201\times{{RE}} }$ = {{I2|A|4}}.
Increase: {{p}} %. With fixed base bias it would have been 100 %!

steps.prompt: A BJT switch has $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}}, $\beta$ = {{beta}}, and the input goes high to {{Vin|V}}. What is the largest $R_B$ that still saturates the transistor?
steps.explanation:
Saturated collector current: $I_{C,sat} = \frac{V_{CC} - 0.2}{R_C}$ = {{ICs|A}}.
Saturation needs $\beta I_B \ge I_{C,sat}$, so $I_B \ge$ {{IBm|A}}.
$R_B \le \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_{B,min}} = \frac{ {{Vin-0.7}} }{ {{IBm}} }$ = {{(Vin-0.7)/IBm|Ω}}. In practice choose a few times smaller for margin.

steps.prompt: In the switch circuit, $v_{in}$ = 5 V, $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}}, $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}}, $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}} and $\beta$ = 100. Find $I_C$.
steps.explanation:
$I_B = (5 - 0.7)/{{RB}}$ = {{IB|A}}. If active, $I_C = \beta I_B$ = {{100*IB|A}} and $V_{CE} = {{VCC}} - {{RC}}\times I_C$ = {{VCC-RC*100*IB|V}} < 0.2 V: impossible.
So the BJT is saturated: $I_C = \frac{V_{CC} - 0.2}{R_C}$ = {{(VCC-0.2)/RC|A}}, and indeed $\beta I_B > I_C$.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of large-signal DC analysis of a BJT circuit in order
items: Assume an operating region (cutoff, active or saturation)
Replace the BJT by the model for that region
Check the constraints of the assumed region
If a constraint fails, assume another region and repeat
steps.explanation: This is the same assume-and-check method as for diodes. For the active region the constraints are $I_B > 0$ and $V_{CE} > 0.2$ V; for saturation $I_B > 0$ and $\beta I_B > I_C > 0$.

steps.prompt: A pnp transistor has $I_B$ = {{IB|A}} (out of the base) and $V_{CE}$ = {{VCE}} V. In which region is it?
steps.explanation: For a pnp the signs flip: active requires $I_B > 0$ and $V_{CE} < -0.2$ V. Here $V_{CE}$ = {{VCE}} V is well below −0.2 V and $I_B > 0$, so it is **active**. (Saturation would show $V_{CE} \approx -0.2$ V.)

steps.title: Output characteristics
steps.body:
The output characteristics show $i_C$ versus $v_{CE}$, with one curve per base current.
- **Active:** the flat part. $i_C = \beta i_B$ hardly depends on $v_{CE}$.
- **Saturation:** the steep part at $v_{CE}$ below a few tenths of a volt.
- **Cutoff:** $i_B$ = 0, so $i_C$ = 0 (along the axis).

steps.prompt: The graph shows the output characteristics of an npn transistor. Find its current gain $\beta$.
steps.explanation: In the active region (the flat part) $i_C = \beta i_B$. The top curve, $i_B$ = {{4*dB|A}}, is flat at {{4*beta*dB|A}}, so $\beta$ = {{4*beta*dB|A}} / {{4*dB|A}} = {{beta}}. Every curve gives the same ratio, e.g. {{beta*dB|A}} / {{dB|A}}.

steps.prompt: In which region does the npn transistor operate at point P? (The grey line along the axis is the curve for $i_B$ = 0.)
steps.explanation:
- **Active:** on the flat part of a curve, where $i_C = \beta i_B$ hardly depends on $v_{CE}$.
- **Saturation:** on the steep part near the vertical axis ($v_{CE}$ ≈ 0.1–0.2 V), where $i_C < \beta i_B$.
- **Cutoff:** on the $i_B$ = 0 curve, so $i_C$ = 0.
P is at $v_{CE}$ ≈ {{px||2}} V.

steps.prompt: The base current of this npn is {{k*dB|A}}. The curves are for $i_B$ = 10, 20, 30 and 40 µA (bottom to top); the orange line is the load line of the collector circuit.
steps.explanation: The Q point is where the load line crosses the curve for $i_B$ = {{k*dB|A}}: $i_C$ ≈ {{iQ|A}}, $v_{CE}$ ≈ {{vQ|V}}. Check: $v_{CE} = V_{CC} - R_Ci_C$ = {{VCC|V}} − {{RC|Ω}} × {{iQ|A}} = {{vQ|V}}. The load line runs from $V_{CC}$ on the $v_{CE}$ axis to $V_{CC}/R_C$ = {{VCC/RC|A}} on the $i_C$ axis.

steps.prompt: A BJT switch drives a load resistor $R_C$ from $V_{CC}$. The line is its load line. At which point does the transistor act as a **closed** switch?
steps.explanation: A closed switch has almost no voltage across it and passes the largest current: the top-left end of the load line, with $v_{CE}$ ≈ 0.2 V and $i_C$ ≈ $(V_{CC} - 0.2)/R_C$ = {{(VCC-0.2)/RC|A}}. That is saturation. The bottom-right end ($i_C$ = 0, $v_{CE} = V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}) is cutoff, an open switch. Points in between are in the active region, where amplifiers work.
